title: Sepsis: the 6 actions in the first hour
bullet1: Suspect sepsis in any patient with NEWS2 >=5 or clinical concern
bullet2: #Take blood cultures before antibiotics — do not delay for more than 45 minutes
bullet3: #Give IV antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition
bullet4: #Measure lactate and send FBC / CRP / CMP
bullet5: #Give IV fluid bolus if lactate above 2 or hypotension present
bullet7: Escalate early — if not improving at 1 hour call critical care
question: A 62-year-old has NEWS2 of 6 and is confused. Which action is the single most time-critical?
optionA: Give furosemide to treat fluid overload
optionC: Wait for blood culture results before any treatment
explanation: Antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition are the most time-critical action. Blood cultures should be taken first but must not delay antibiotic administration beyond 45 minutes.
source_title: Sepsis-6 and NICE NG51 — sepsis recognition

title: Paediatric acute wheeze: initial assessment and severity scoring
bullet1: Use a validated severity score (e.g. PRAM or modified Borg) at presentation and after treatment
bullet2: #Bronchodilators first: salbutamol via MDI+spacer is as effective as nebulised in mild-moderate wheeze
bullet3: #Add ipratropium bromide to every nebulisation in moderate or severe wheeze
bullet4: #IV magnesium sulphate 40 mg/kg (max 2 g) IV over 20 min in severe or life-threatening wheeze
bullet5: Steroids early — oral prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg (max 40 mg) as soon as wheeze recognised
bullet6: Escalate if SpO2 persistently below 92% or exhaustion develops
bullet7: A 5-year-old with moderate acute wheeze has had two salbutamol spacer doses. What should be added for the next cycle?
question: Oral montelukast
optionB: Ipratropium bromide with the next salbutamol dose
answer: Ipratropium bromide is added to every nebulisation in moderate and severe paediatric wheeze. IV aminophylline is a later step; montelukast has no role in acute management.
explanation: British Guideline on the Management of Asthma (BTS/SIGN)
